blocks.text: Every host has to answer one basic question before it can do anything useful, which servers should I even talk to. The simplest answer is to just write the list down by hand and load it at startup.
But a fixed list only works if the world stays still. Once the servers a task might need change more often than a config file does, something has to find them instead of a person writing them down.
That something is dynamic server discovery, and it trades a comfortable certainty for a new kind of risk, which this topic walks through carefully.
1. The Static Server List: Manual and Fixed

blocks.alt: The Static Server List: Manual and Fixed
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163540-129957684.png

The most common way to connect a host to MCP servers today is a plain configuration file. Someone writes down a name, a command or URL, and maybe some environment variables, for each server the host should know about.
This list does not change unless a person edits it. If a new server comes online somewhere on the network, the host has no idea it exists until someone adds it to the file and restarts.
That sounds limiting, but it is also exactly why static lists are so common. A human looked at every entry before it went in.
1.1 Why teams still choose the static approach
For a small, fixed set of internal tools, a static list is simple to reason about. There is no query to fail, no registry to keep running, and no surprise entry showing up overnight.

items: Every server was reviewed by a person before being added.
The list is easy to read, audit, and diff in version control.
Nothing can change behavior without a deliberate edit and a restart.

blocks.text: 2. What Changes With Dynamic Discovery
Dynamic discovery flips the arrangement around. Instead of a person deciding in advance which servers exist, the host asks a question at runtime and gets an answer back.
The question is usually something like, who out there can handle this kind of task right now. The answer is a list of servers the host did not know about a moment earlier.

Nothing about the wire protocol changes, a discovered server still speaks the same MCP messages as a manually configured one. What changes is only how the host learned that server was worth talking to.
3. Service Registries: A Directory of Available Servers

blocks.alt: Service Registries: A Directory of Available Servers
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163540-702906969.png
A service registry is the piece that makes dynamic discovery possible. It is a directory, servers register themselves into it, and hosts query it to find candidates.
Think of it as a phone book that updates itself. Servers add their own entry when they start up, and the registry is the one place a host needs to check instead of tracking every server individually.

blocks.title: A registry is infrastructure, not part of MCP itself
blocks.content: The MCP specification defines how a host talks to a server once it has decided to connect. It does not define how the host found that server in the first place, discovery and registries sit one layer above the protocol, as surrounding infrastructure a deployment can choose to add.

blocks.text: 3.1 Where a registry typically lives
In a small setup, a registry might just be a shared database one team runs internally. In a larger ecosystem, it can be a public service that many unrelated hosts and servers all point to.
Either way, the registry itself is just another service, it can go down, get out of date, or be queried too slowly, and a host needs to plan for that.
4. What a Registry Entry Contains
A useful registry entry needs more than just an address. It needs enough detail for a host to decide whether this server is even relevant.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Purpose"],"rows":[["name","Human readable identity of the server"],["endpoint","Address or connection details the host will use"],["capabilities","Tags describing what the server can do, for example weather, search, or file access"],["version","Which version of the server is running"],["lastSeen","Timestamp of the most recent heartbeat, used to judge freshness"]]}

blocks.text: Capabilities are the field a host actually filters on. Everything else is detail it needs once a candidate has already been selected.
5. Discovery Protocols: How a Host Finds the Registry Itself
Before a host can query a registry, it has to know the registry exists in the first place. That first step is what a discovery protocol actually solves.

items: A fixed, well known registry address baked into the host, similar to how a browser knows a default search engine.
A broadcast style lookup on the local network, where the host asks who is out there and registries answer.
A directory of directories, one well known top level service that in turn points to other registries.

blocks.text: Whichever method is used, the goal is the same. Get the host from knowing nothing to holding one registry address it can start querying.
Most production setups just hardcode this first address, since it rarely changes, and reserve the dynamic part of discovery for finding servers, not for finding the registry itself.
6. Querying a Registry by Capability
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163540-11805125.png
Once the host has a registry address, the actual query is usually a simple request. It states what capability it needs, and the registry answers with matching servers.
The response is just a list of entries like the ones described earlier, name, endpoint, capabilities, and freshness. Nothing has connected yet, this is only a lookup.
7. Matching Servers to the Current Task
A capability tag on its own is a blunt tool. Several servers might all claim currency conversion, but differ wildly in reliability, speed, or scope.

A good host does not just grab the first entry returned. It looks at the extra fields in each entry, freshness, version, maybe a reported success rate, and picks the candidate that actually fits the task at hand.
8. Registering a Server So It Can Be Found
Discovery only works if servers actually put themselves into the registry. That side of the exchange is called registration.
A server usually sends this payload once at startup, and then keeps sending small heartbeat pings so the registry knows it is still alive.
9. Keeping the Registry Fresh: Health and Liveness

blocks.alt: Keeping the Registry Fresh: Health and Liveness
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163541-920449538.png
A registry entry for a server that crashed an hour ago is worse than no entry at all, because it looks like a valid option.
That is why lastSeen matters so much. A registry usually drops or hides any entry whose heartbeat has gone quiet for too long.
A host querying for candidates should treat freshness as a filter, not just a display field, an old timestamp is a real reason to skip an entry.
9.1 Choosing a freshness window

items: A short window, a few minutes, suits servers that restart often or run on unstable infrastructure.
A longer window, an hour or more, suits stable, long running servers that rarely go down.
Whatever window is picked, it should be shorter than how long a host is willing to wait for a dead connection to time out.

blocks.text: 10. The Trust Problem: Nobody Vetted This Server

blocks.alt: The Trust Problem: Nobody Vetted This Server
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163541-5516638.png
Here is the tradeoff at the center of this whole topic. A manually configured server was chosen by a person, someone looked at it and decided it was safe to add.
A discovered server was chosen by a registry lookup. Nobody on the host side ever laid eyes on it before the connection request went out.

blocks.title: Flexibility and trust pull in opposite directions
blocks.content: The whole appeal of dynamic discovery is reaching servers nobody manually configured. The whole danger of dynamic discovery is reaching servers nobody manually vetted. Those are the same sentence describing the same servers, just from two different angles.

blocks.text: 11. Trust Signals a Registry Can Offer
A registry cannot replace human judgment, but it can carry signals that make automated trust decisions less blind.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal","What it suggests"],"rows":[["Signed registration","The entry came from whoever holds a specific private key, not just anyone"],["Publisher identity","A known organization stands behind this server, not an anonymous entry"],["Community rating or usage count","Many other hosts have connected to this server before"],["Sandboxed by default","A newly discovered server runs with reduced permissions until proven safe"]]}

blocks.text: None of these signals guarantee safety on their own. Together, they give a host something better than a blind coin flip.
12. A Hybrid Approach: Static Trust, Dynamic Reach

blocks.alt: A Hybrid Approach: Static Trust, Dynamic Reach
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163541-538181947.png
Most real deployments do not pick one extreme. They keep a small static list of servers that always get full trust, and layer dynamic discovery on top for everything else.

items: Core, sensitive servers stay in the manually vetted static list, for example anything touching payments or private files.
Discovered servers are only allowed to run with reduced permissions, for example read only, no file access.
A discovered server can be promoted into the trusted static list later, once a person has actually reviewed it.

blocks.text: This way, flexibility applies where the stakes are low, and manual vetting still guards anything that really matters.
13. Revoking Access When a Discovered Server Turns Out Bad

blocks.alt: Revoking Access When a Discovered Server Turns Out Bad
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163860-900462440.png
Trust decisions made at discovery time are not permanent. A server that looked fine an hour ago can start behaving badly, or simply turn out to have been malicious all along.
A host that supports discovery needs a fast way to cut off a specific server, closing any open session and refusing to reconnect to it, without needing a full restart.

blocks.title: Revocation should be as easy as connection
blocks.content: If adding a discovered server takes one query but removing a bad one takes a manual code change and a deploy, the system is lopsided in exactly the wrong direction.

blocks.text: 14. Caching Discovery Results Between Task Runs
Querying a registry on every single task is wasteful if the same capability keeps coming up. Most hosts cache recent discovery results for a short period.
A cache has to respect the same freshness rules as a live query though, a cached entry pointing at a server that has since gone quiet is just as misleading as a stale registry entry.

items: Cache the list of candidate servers for a given capability, not just a single chosen server.
Expire cache entries at least as aggressively as the registry expires its own stale entries.
Re-check trust signals on a cache hit, do not skip that step just because the lookup itself was skipped.

blocks.text: 15. Worked Example: A Host Discovers a Currency Conversion Server
A travel planning assistant needs to convert prices between currencies, a capability it was never configured with in advance.

items: 1. The host queries its known registry for the capability currency-conversion.
2. The registry returns two candidates, fx-rates-server and quick-fx-server.
3. The host checks lastSeen on both, quick-fx-server has not sent a heartbeat in six hours and is dropped.
4. The host checks fx-rates-server for a signed registration and finds one from a recognized publisher.
5. The host connects to fx-rates-server, but only grants it read only, no file or network side effects beyond the conversion call.
6. The conversion result comes back, and the connection is treated as untrusted for anything beyond this one task.

blocks.text: Nothing here required a person to have configured fx-rates-server in advance, yet the host still made a reasoned, cautious decision instead of blindly trusting the first result.
16. Common Mistakes With Dynamic Discovery

items: Connecting to the first server a registry returns without checking freshness or trust signals at all.
Granting a discovered server the same full permissions a manually vetted server would get.
Treating an old, stale registry entry as if it were still a live and reachable server.
Assuming a registry itself is inherently trustworthy just because it is the one the host happened to be configured with.
Never promoting a repeatedly useful discovered server into a properly reviewed, trusted list.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes come from treating discovery as a shortcut past trust decisions, rather than as a step that still needs one.
17. Practice: Design a Capability Query
Given a registry that exposes a servers endpoint filtered by capability, write the client side lookup a host would run before connecting to anything.
Notice the filter keeps only signed, recently seen entries. That single line is where the trust tradeoff actually gets enforced in code.
Key Takeaway

A static server list is safe because a person looked at every entry, and dynamic discovery is flexible because a registry can find servers no person ever saw in advance, and a host that wants both has to keep checking trust signals even after a lookup succeeds.

Discovery answers the question of reach, whether a host can find a server it did not know about. It never answers the separate question of trust, and treating those as the same question is the mistake this whole topic guards against.
